Christianity.description: The dominant religion in Russia during the 19th century, central to the spiritual and philosophical dilemmas faced by the characters.

fur cloak.description: A luxurious and warm outer garment made of animal fur, typical of Russian aristocracy.

muslin garment.description: A lightweight, thin piece of clothing made from muslin, a fine cotton fabric.

Spinoza.description: Baruch Spinoza, a 17th-century Dutch philosopher known for his rationalist and pantheistic ideas.

Kant.description: Immanuel Kant, an 18th-century German philosopher known for his work on epistemology and ethics.

Schelling.description: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling, a German idealist philosopher.

Hegel.description: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, a German philosopher influential in idealism and dialectics.

Schopenhauer.description: Arthur Schopenhauer, a German philosopher known for his pessimistic philosophy and concept of the 'will.'

Homiakov.description: Aleksey Khomyakov, a Russian theologian and philosopher associated with the Slavophile movement and Orthodox Christian thought.

Greek orthodox.description: Refers to the Eastern Orthodox Church, particularly the Greek tradition, one of the main branches of Christianity.

doctrine.description: A set of beliefs or teachings, especially those held and promoted by a religious or philosophical group.

redemption.description: In Christian theology, the act of being saved from sin, error, or evil.

infallible.description: Incapable of making mistakes or being wrong, often used in reference to religious authority.

edifice.description: A complex system of beliefs or arguments, metaphorically described as a building or structure.

pothouse.description: A tavern or drinking establishment, often frequented by peasants and sometimes a source of income for landowners.

keeper.description: An employee responsible for looking after a particular part of the estate, such as game, livestock, or property.

Matrona.description: An old peasant woman, referred to as Levin's old friend whom he once helped after an accident.

Platon.description: A wise and well-to-do peasant whose simple faith inspires Levin's spiritual awakening.

Kirillov.description: A former house porter who now rents land that once belonged to a cooperative association.

Mituh.description: A contemptuous nickname used by the peasants for Kirillov.

fallows.description: Fields left unplanted for a period to restore their fertility.

thrash.description: To separate grain from the husks and straw, typically using a machine or by hand.

sheaf.description: A bundle of grain stalks tied together after reaping.

aspen.description: A type of tree commonly used in Russian rural construction.

thatch.description: A roof covering made of straw, reeds, or similar materials.

seed-corn.description: Grain reserved for planting the next crop, not for eating.

barn.description: A farm building used for storing grain, hay, and housing livestock.

thrasher.description: A person or machine that separates grain from the husks and straw.

cooperative association.description: A group of peasants or workers who jointly manage and benefit from land or resources.

house porter.description: A servant or caretaker in a large household, often responsible for maintenance and security.

flay the skin off.description: An idiom meaning to be extremely harsh or merciless, especially in collecting debts.

wring the last penny out.description: An idiom meaning to extract the maximum possible payment, often ruthlessly.

Master.description: A term used by Levin to refer to a higher spiritual authority or God, indicating submission and guidance.

couch-grass.description: A common Eurasian grass (Elymus repens), often considered a weed in fields and pastures.

goat-weed.description: A common name for various wild plants; here, it refers to a plant found in Russian meadows.

noose.description: A loop with a slipknot, here referring to a knot Levin ties with blades of grass.

neighbor.description: Used in the Biblical sense, meaning fellow human beings whom one is commanded to love.

Creator.description: A term for God, emphasizing the divine role as maker of the universe.

Creation.description: The religious doctrine describing God's creation of the world, a subject of Levin's philosophical questioning.

The devil.description: The embodiment of evil in Christian theology, referenced in Levin's internal debate.

atonement.description: A Christian doctrine concerning reconciliation with God, often through Christ's sacrifice.

syringe.description: A tube with a nozzle and piston for squirting liquids, here used by children for play.

crockery.description: Dishes, cups, and other tableware made of earthenware or china.

imbeciles.description: An outdated term for people with intellectual disabilities, used here to mean 'simple-minded people.'

destiny.description: A person's fate or predetermined course of events, often with spiritual connotations.

Kolok.description: A copse (small wooded area) near Levin's house, where Kitty has taken Mitya.

Spencer.description: Herbert Spencer, a prominent English philosopher and sociologist whose works influenced Russian intellectuals.

shafts.description: The long poles between which a horse is harnessed to a carriage.

haunches.description: The hindquarters or upper part of a horse's back legs.

ice cellar.description: An underground storage room used to keep food cool before refrigeration.

sunshade.description: A parasol or umbrella used to protect from the sun.

heart’s-ease.description: A common name for the wild pansy flower.

hellebore.description: A type of perennial plant, often found in Russian meadows.

drone.description: A male bee, whose primary role is to mate with the queen.

bee-keeper.description: A person who keeps and cares for bees, also known as an apiarist.

Ivan Ivanovitch Ragozov.description: A character mentioned as a possible instigator of war, likely a satirical reference.

Mihalitch.description: A respectful form of address for a peasant or servant, here referring to a local beekeeper.

Alexander Nikolaevitch.description: Refers to Alexander II, Emperor of Russia at the time.

Pogatchev.description: Refers to Yemelyan Pugachev, leader of a major Cossack rebellion in Russia in the 18th century.

Khiva.description: A Central Asian khanate, site of Russian military campaigns in the 19th century.

honeycomb.description: A structure of hexagonal cells made by bees to store honey and larvae.

aspen leaf.description: A leaf from the aspen tree, used here as a makeshift surface.

Slavs.description: Ethnic group of peoples in Eastern Europe sharing similar languages and cultural heritage.

sons of Hagar.description: Biblical reference used here to describe Muslims, specifically the Turks, in a pejorative way.

Bulgarian atrocities.description: Refers to massacres and violence against Bulgarians under Ottoman rule, which shocked European opinion in the 1870s.

ne’er-do-wells.description: People regarded as lazy or irresponsible; good-for-nothings.

Alphonse Karr.description: A French journalist and novelist, quoted here for his satirical comment on war.

Varyagi.description: The Varangians, Norse warriors who were invited to rule over the early Russian state, referenced here as a historical tradition.

press.description: Refers to newspapers and journalists collectively.

grape-shot.description: A type of ammunition used in cannons, consisting of small iron balls, used here metaphorically.

advance-guards.description: Soldiers positioned at the front of an army, leading an attack.

phenomenon.description: An observable event or occurrence, often used here to describe a notable social trend.

oak tree.description: A specific, familiar tree in the copse that is struck by lightning during the storm.

servants’ quarters.description: The area of a large household where the domestic staff live and take shelter.

kerchiefs.description: Square pieces of cloth used as head coverings or for protection against the rain.

perambulator.description: A baby carriage or pram, used for transporting infants.

burdocks.description: Large-leaved plants common in Russia, often found in the countryside.

Eastern question.description: A 19th-century diplomatic issue concerning the decline of the Ottoman Empire and the interests of European powers in its territories.

Christian church.description: Refers to the collective body of Christian denominations, especially in the context of Russian Orthodoxy.

Buddhists.description: Followers of Buddhism, a major world religion originating in Asia.

Mohammedans.description: An archaic term for Muslims, followers of Islam.

Slavonic race.description: Refers to the Slavic peoples of Eastern Europe, including Russians, Poles, Czechs, and others.

oak.description: A type of tree; here, likely refers to a specific oak tree on the estate, often symbolizing strength or endurance.

cook.description: A household servant responsible for preparing meals, common in aristocratic Russian households.

the church.description: Refers to the Christian Church, representing organized religion and the community of believers.

the Jews.description: Refers to followers of Judaism, one of the major world religions.

the Mohammedans.description: An older term for Muslims, followers of Islam.

the Confucians.description: Followers of Confucianism, a philosophical and ethical system based on the teachings of Confucius.

the Buddhists.description: Followers of Buddhism, a major world religion originating in Asia.

lime trees.description: A type of tree common in Russian estates, known for its fragrant flowers.

Milky Way.description: The galaxy containing our solar system, visible as a band of light in the night sky.

meridian.description: An imaginary line on the earth's surface from the North Pole to the South Pole, used in astronomy and geography.

horizon.description: The line at which the earth's surface and the sky appear to meet.

wash stand.description: A piece of furniture with a basin and pitcher for washing, common before indoor plumbing.

holy of holies.description: A biblical term for the innermost and most sacred area of a temple, used metaphorically here for the most private part of one's soul.
